sentences.text: Imperobator stands as one of only two non-avian theropod dinosaurs known from Antarctica.

The holotype specimen, which serves as the primary reference for the species, consists of an incomplete isolated left foot including part of the shin bone, ankle bones, and toe claws, along with teeth and skull fragments.
Additional fossils associated with the original specimen include skull fragments, a tail vertebra, more teeth, and foot elements held by other institutions.
While the holotype measures approximately 45 centimeters in length, reexaminations of specific bones revised the estimated body length of the animal to between 2 and 3 meters.
The dinosaur possesses a unique trait where the ankle bones, known as calcanea, are fused with the fibulae.
Metatarsal II of Imperobator is unique among paravians for its parallelogram-shaped cross-section.
The fossils were unearthed in December 2003 by an expedition mounted by the University of California Museum of Paleontology on the Naze Peninsula of James Ross Island, Antarctica.
These remains belong to the Cape Lamb Member of the Snow Hill Island Formation, dating to approximately 71 million years ago in the early Maastrichtian.
Ricardo Ely and Judd Case formally described Imperobator antarcticus as a new genus and species in 2019, giving the name meaning 'powerful warrior' in Latin.
Imperobator is classified within the clade Paraves rather than Dromaeosauridae due to traits such as the absence of a sickle claw and a smooth distal metatarsal II.

Before its official description, a 2007 paper assigned the specimen to the clade Dromaeosauridae, but the specimen lacked key dromaeosaurid traits, such as a prominent sickle claw, making that initial assignment problematic.

The formal description assigned Imperobator to the clade Paraves, and a 2019 analysis by Hartman et al. recovered Imperobator as a basal deinonychosaur outside the subgroups Dromaeosauridae, Unenlagiinae, and Troodontidae.
Researchers studying the unenlagiine Diuqin in 2024 considered Imperobator to be a possible member of that group.
Despite the scientific consensus shifting toward Paraves, the Paleobi Database lists the parent group of Imperobator as Dromaeosauridae and classifies the animal within the family Dromaeosauridae.
Imperobator lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically the Maastrichtian age, inhabiting what is now James Ross Island in Antarctica.
The animal lived during the Maastrichtian stage, between 72.2 and 66 million years ago.
Fossils of Imperobator are found only in the Cape Lamb Member of the Snow Hill Island Formation on James Ross Island, Antarctica.

The habitat where Imperobator lived resembled modern high-latitude volcanic arches in terms of flora, climate, and environment. During the Maastrichtian, the Antarctic Peninsula lacked large ice sheets due to a warmer and more humid global climate.
The environment was dominated by Gondwanan subpolar forests containing both conifers and angiosperms.
Imperobator crossed to Antarctica when the continent was still part of the supercontinent Gondwana.
Surface weathering on Imperobator fossils suggests they experienced minimal transport or reworking after death.
There is a debate regarding the size of Imperobator; while initially thought to be as large as Utahraptor, later revisions suggest it was smaller, comparable to Neuquenraptor and Deinonychus.
It is debated whether Imperobator is a dromaeosaur, as the fossil foot lacks the distinct sickle claw typical of that group.
A 2025 study raised doubts about the identification of certain leg bones, suggesting they might be fragments of metatarsals rather than the tibia and ankle bones originally described.
It is debated whether Imperobator belongs to Dromaeosauridae or Unenlagiinae, with recent analyses supporting the latter.
